::: {.exercise-lead}
This study follows recorded armed conflict across Myanmar’s 330 townships from January 2021 to September 2025, with a closer look at events targeting civilians.
:::

[View the executive summary](take-home-exercise-02-summary.qmd)

## Introduction {#study-questions}

### Conflict in Myanmar

Myanmar’s armed conflicts predate the military coup of February 2021. For decades, ethnic armed organisations fought for greater autonomy. After the coup, new resistance groups emerged and fighting spread into central areas that had experienced relative peace. [ACLED’s background report](https://acleddata.com/report/between-cooperation-and-competition-struggle-resistance-groups-myanmar) describes how these groups cooperate and compete across different regions.

The consequences reach well beyond the places where fighting is recorded. In December 2024, OCHA estimated that almost **3.5 million people were displaced within Myanmar**. Its [2025 humanitarian response plan](https://myanmar.un.org/en/286727-myanmar-humanitarian-needs-and-response-plan-2025-december-2024) describes families struggling to find food and shelter, with education and healthcare severely disrupted.

Reading this background, I find it difficult to equate a fall in reported violence with recovery. Families may still be unable to return home or get the care they need. I want to keep those continuing needs in view as I compare the townships.

### What this study examines

For the [Geospatial Analytics for Peace assignment](https://isss626-ay2026-27aug.netlify.app/take-home_ex02), I combine ACLED’s event records with township boundaries. I start with the national timeline, then look more closely at individual townships and their neighbours. Returning to the monthly histories helps distinguish places with years of recorded fighting from those with a more recent increase.

These comparisons can help aid organisations choose where to check for growing or continuing needs. I focus on three questions:

- Which townships form clusters of high recorded conflict, and which stand out from their neighbours?
- Where have hotspots appeared, continued or weakened over the study period?
- Does the pattern change when I focus on civilian targeting or reported deaths?

### National trends and local differences

The national total fell by **12.4%** between January–September 2024 and the same months of 2025. Over that comparison, **127 townships recorded increases**. Events targeting civilians fell by only **2%**.

Kawkareik and Nawnghkio each recorded more events by September 2025 than in all of 2024. Monywa has the largest total across the full study period. These different histories are worth following separately when considering where support may still be needed.

### Which events are included?


```{r}
#| label: th02-filter
#| eval: false
```

I exclude six “Indian Ocean” records, protests and strategic developments. The study keeps **battles, explosions/remote violence, and violence against civilians**.

Of the 54,000 qualifying records, 107 have no named township and 88 have only a broad location. Removing them leaves **`r fmt(a$validation$retained)` events**, with no duplicate IDs.


```{r}
#| label: th02-coordinates
#| eval: false
```

I match each township with its state or region, allowing for spelling and punctuation differences, including “Pangsang (Panghkam)”. This avoids assigning city-wide reports to a city-centre point. For `r a$validation$coordinate_disagreements` records, the coordinates fall outside the named township. I keep the named township and log these cases without changing the raw data.

::: {.callout-note title="What the counts mean"}
Reporting coverage varies, so event counts cannot measure risk per person or capture all violence. ACLED flags events where civilians were the main or only target; other incidents may also harm civilians. [ACLED codebook](https://acleddata.com/methodology/acled-codebook)
:::

### Keeping months with no recorded events {#preparing-the-monthly-data}


```{r}
#| label: th02-cube
#| eval: false
```

Each township gets one row per month: **330 × 57 = 18,810 rows**. Months without a qualifying event keep a zero count. They make up `r pct(a$validation$zero_event_bins/a$validation$bins)` of the rows, so dropping them would leave out much of the quieter period.

The analysis uses the same boundary version throughout. The monthly comparison also avoids treating the nine months of 2025 as a full year.

## Where and when conflict was recorded

I first look at the timing of recorded violence across Myanmar. This gives some context for the township comparisons that follow.

![Monthly counts of battles, explosions and remote violence, and violence against civilians.](take-home-02/figures/monthly.png)

The highest monthly total is **November 2023, with 1,465 events**, followed by December with 1,447. Counts remain high into early 2024. Explosions and remote violence account for the largest category in both 2024 and the available months of 2025.

The peak came shortly after Operation 1027 began in northern Shan on 27 October 2023. [ACLED’s account of that month](https://acleddata.com/update/regional-overview-asia-pacific-october-2023) describes a sharp escalation in fighting following the Brotherhood Alliance’s offensive.

January–September 2025 has **8,728 events**, compared with **9,961** in the same months of 2024: a **12.4% decline**.

### Where the national decline came from {#recent-township-changes}

To see where the national decline came from, I compare January to September in both years and map each township’s change. Keeping the same months gives each year an equal observation period.

```{r}
#| label: th02-recent-counts
recent_counts <- a$cube %>%
  filter(lubridate::year(month) %in% 2024:2025,
         lubridate::month(month) <= 9) %>%
  mutate(year = lubridate::year(month)) %>%
  group_by(TS_PCODE, year) %>%
  summarise(events = sum(events), civilian = sum(civilian), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = c(events, civilian))

recent <- a$towns %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST) %>%
  left_join(recent_counts, by = "TS_PCODE") %>%
  mutate(change = events_2025 - events_2024,
         civilian_change = civilian_2025 - civilian_2024)
```

```{r}
#| label: th02-recent-map
change_map <- a$towns %>%
  select(TS_PCODE) %>%
  left_join(recent, by = "TS_PCODE")
change_limit <- ceiling(max(abs(recent$change)) / 50) * 50
p_change_map <- ggplot(change_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = change), colour = "white", linewidth = .08) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "RdBu", direction = -1,
                       limits = c(-change_limit, change_limit),
                       breaks = c(-change_limit, 0, change_limit), name = "Change in events") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(title = "Where counts rose and fell")

largest_changes <- bind_rows(
  slice_max(recent, change, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE),
  slice_min(recent, change, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE)) %>%
  mutate(label = paste(TS, ST, sep = " · "))
p_change_bar <- ggplot(largest_changes, aes(change, reorder(label, change))) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = change), width = .65, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "RdBu", direction = -1,
                       limits = c(-change_limit, change_limit)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey55", linewidth = .3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%+d", change), hjust = if_else(change > 0, -.12, 1.12)),
            size = 3.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = .2)) +
  labs(x = "2025 count minus 2024 count", y = NULL, title = "Five largest rises and falls") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9))
change_figure <- p_change_map + p_change_bar + patchwork::plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.35)) +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(subtitle = "January to September in both years")
ggsave("take-home-02/figures/recent-changes.png", change_figure,
       width = 11, height = 7, dpi = 170, bg = "white")
```

![Changes in recorded events, comparing January to September 2024 with the same months of 2025. Red indicates an increase; blue indicates a decrease.](take-home-02/figures/recent-changes.png)

Counts rose in **`r sum(recent$change > 0)` townships**, fell in `r sum(recent$change < 0)`, and stayed the same in `r sum(recent$change == 0)`. The increases added `r fmt(sum(pmax(recent$change, 0)))` events; the decreases removed `r fmt(-sum(pmin(recent$change, 0)))`. Their difference produces the national fall of `r fmt(-sum(recent$change))`.

Kawkareik rose from **122 to 356**, Kyaukpyu from **56 to 263**, and Nawnghkio from **202 to 341**. Rakhine’s total fell by 734, even as Kyaukpyu, within Rakhine, had the second-largest township increase. A regional decline can therefore leave individual communities facing more recorded conflict.

### Maungdaw ranks much higher for reported deaths {#events-and-reported-deaths}

So far, every incident has counted equally. I also want to understand where the loss of life was greatest, since a smaller number of incidents can still have devastating consequences. Following the comparison of different measures in [Christover Manafe’s study](https://isss626-camanafe.netlify.app/take_home_ex/take_home_ex02/take_home_ex02#feature-engineering), I examine reported deaths alongside incident counts.

```{r}
#| label: th02-fatality-counts
fatality_counts <- a$towns %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST, events, fatalities) %>%
  mutate(event_rank = min_rank(desc(events)),
         fatality_rank = min_rank(desc(fatalities)))
fatality_examples <- fatality_counts %>%
  filter(TS %in% c("Monywa", "Kale", "Maungdaw"))
```

```{r}
#| label: th02-fatality-plot
p_death_map <- ggplot(a$towns) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = fatalities), colour = "white", linewidth = .06) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlOrRd", direction = 1,
                       trans = "sqrt", breaks = c(0, 500, 1800), labels = scales::comma,
                       name = "Reported deaths") +
  guides(fill = guide_colourbar(title.position = "top", barwidth = grid::unit(4.5, "cm"))) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(title = "Where deaths were reported")
p_death_comparison <- ggplot(fatality_counts, aes(events, fatalities)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey65", size = 1.8, alpha = .6) +
  geom_point(data = fatality_examples, colour = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = fatality_examples, aes(label = TS), hjust = 1.1, vjust = -.7, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(.03, .12))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(.03, .12))) +
  labs(x = "Recorded events", y = "Reported deaths",
       title = "Incidents and reported deaths", subtitle = "Each dot is one township")
fatality_figure <- p_death_map + p_death_comparison +
  patchwork::plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.2)) +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(subtitle = "January 2021 to September 2025")
ggsave("take-home-02/figures/events-and-deaths.png", fatality_figure,
       width = 11, height = 7, dpi = 170, bg = "white")
```

![Reported deaths by township, alongside the relationship between event counts and reported deaths. Monywa, Kale and Maungdaw are labelled.](take-home-02/figures/events-and-deaths.png)

**Maungdaw ranks 17th by incidents but third by reported deaths:** 599 events and 1,583 deaths. **Kale has the highest reported death toll, at 1,877**, although its 886 events place it fourth by incident count. Monywa leads the event count with 1,039 and ranks second for reported deaths, at 1,771.

This comparison makes me wary of using incident counts alone to decide where to assess needs first. Maungdaw could receive less attention that way, even with its high reported death toll. I would want local clinics and aid groups to help assess what affected households need there and in Kale.

The reported death estimates cover all retained conflict events, including combatant deaths; they are not civilian death totals. ACLED records zero when no fatality information is available, so zero does not establish that nobody died. [ACLED codebook](https://acleddata.com/methodology/acled-codebook)

## Where conflict forms clusters {#clusters-outliers-and-hotspots}

The totals show which townships recorded more conflict. I next look at whether nearby townships share that pattern. Local Moran’s I distinguishes clusters from places that stand out from their neighbours, while Gi* identifies concentrations of high or low counts across a neighbourhood.

### What counts as a neighbour?


```{r}
#| label: th02-neighbours
#| eval: false
```

I start with **Queen contiguity**: townships are neighbours if their boundaries touch at an edge or corner. Each township’s neighbour weights sum to one. Local Moran’s I compares the township with those neighbours; Gi* also includes the township itself.

Chaungzon, Munaung and Cocokyun have no shared-boundary neighbours in this layer. Their counts remain in the study, but I leave them unclassified in the Queen-based tests. I use an Albers projection centred on Myanmar for mapping and distance checks, with a one-metre tolerance when identifying shared boundaries.


```{r}
#| label: th02-local-tests
#| eval: false
```

Both tests use 999 conditional permutations: counts are shuffled among other townships while the focal count stays fixed. The maps show **two-sided permutation p < 0.05**; grey areas are not significant.

### Most hotspots are in central Myanmar


```{r}
#| label: th02-local-run
#| eval: false
```

```{r}
#| label: th02-map-style
#| eval: false
```

```{r}
#| label: th02-local-plot
#| eval: false
```

![Local Moran’s I clusters and outliers alongside Getis–Ord Gi-star hotspots and coldspots.](take-home-02/figures/local-association.png)

Local Moran’s I identifies **38 high–high townships, 52 low–low townships and four low–high outliers**. The outliers are Hlaingbwe, Tonzang, Seikphyu and Pyinoolwin: their own counts are below the township average, but their neighbours’ weighted counts are above it. No high–low outlier passes the significance threshold. Gi* identifies **38 hotspots and 53 coldspots**.

**Sagaing has 18 Gi* hotspots, Mandalay seven and Magway six.** Both methods point to central Myanmar, though their different tests give slightly different low-count classifications.

Of the **53 Gi* coldspots**, 13 are in Ayeyarwady, 11 in Yangon and ten in Shan (East). These neighbourhoods have relatively low recorded counts across the full study period. Local Moran’s I places most low–low clusters in the same areas.

Kawkareik ranks second with **946 events**, yet its whole-period Gi* result is not significant. Much of its increase came late in the study.

```{r}
#| label: th02-local-counts
lisa_counts <- a$local %>%
  count(lisa, name = "Townships") %>%
  rename(Result = lisa) %>%
  mutate(Method = "Local Moran’s I")

hotspot_counts <- a$local %>%
  count(gi_cluster, name = "Townships") %>%
  rename(Result = gi_cluster) %>%
  mutate(Method = "Gi*")

bind_rows(lisa_counts, hotspot_counts) %>%
  select(Method, Result, Townships) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

### Which hotspots survive stricter checks? {#how-much-do-the-choices-matter}


```{r}
#| label: th02-neighbour-checks
#| eval: false
```

Before using these labels to shortlist townships, I check how much they depend on the analysis choices. I repeat Gi* with a symmetric six-nearest-centroid neighbourhood and with only the more precisely located records. I also apply the Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment because testing many townships can produce chance discoveries.

```{r}
#| label: th02-sensitivity
tibble(Check = c("Queen neighbours", "Queen neighbours, multiple-test adjustment", "Six nearest neighbours", "Queen neighbours, precise locations only"),
       Hotspots = c(sum(hot), sum(hot & a$local$gi_q < .05, na.rm = TRUE),
                    sum(a$comparison$knn6[valid] == "Hotspot"), sum(a$comparison$precise_only == "Hotspot")),
       Coldspots = c(sum(a$local$gi_cluster == "Coldspot"), sum(a$local$gi_cluster == "Coldspot" & a$local$gi_q < .05, na.rm = TRUE),
                     sum(a$comparison$knn6[valid] == "Coldspot"), sum(a$comparison$precise_only == "Coldspot"))) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

The multiple-test adjustment reduces the hotspot count from **38 to 19**. I therefore treat the wider unadjusted hotspot map as exploratory. Across the 327 townships with Queen neighbours, the hotspot/coldspot/non-significant classifications agree in **87.2%** of cases with six-nearest neighbours and **91.7%** when only more precise locations are retained.

The broad pattern holds, though individual labels change and six-nearest neighbours produces more coldspots. I keep shared boundaries for the main analysis.

### Some increases sit among declining neighbours {#changes-and-neighbours}

Kyaukpyu’s rise within a declining region made me want to look more closely at its neighbours. I compare each township’s recent change with the average change among its Queen neighbours, excluding itself. The three island townships remain outside this comparison.

```{r}
#| label: th02-change-lag
library(spdep)
change_weights <- nb2listw(a$nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
recent$neighbour_change <- lag.listw(change_weights, recent$change, zero.policy = TRUE)
has_neighbours <- card(a$nb) > 0
recent$neighbour_change[!has_neighbours] <- NA_real_

set.seed(62603)
change_moran <- moran.mc(recent$change[has_neighbours],
                         nb2listw(subset(a$nb, has_neighbours), style = "W"),
                         nsim = 999, alternative = "greater")
```

```{r}
#| label: th02-change-lag-plot
neighbour_changes <- recent %>%
  filter(!is.na(neighbour_change)) %>%
  mutate(direction = case_when(
    change > 0 & neighbour_change > 0 ~ "Both increased",
    change > 0 & neighbour_change < 0 ~ "Township up, neighbours down",
    change < 0 & neighbour_change > 0 ~ "Township down, neighbours up",
    change < 0 & neighbour_change < 0 ~ "Both decreased",
    TRUE ~ "One or both unchanged"))
p_change_lag <- ggplot(neighbour_changes, aes(change, neighbour_change)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey65", linewidth = .4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey65", linewidth = .4) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = direction), size = 2.1, alpha = .7) +
  geom_text(data = filter(neighbour_changes, TS %in% c("Kyaukpyu", "Kawkareik", "Nawnghkio")),
            aes(label = TS), hjust = 1.08, vjust = -.6, size = 3.4) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Change in the township’s count", y = "Average change among its neighbours",
       title = "Township changes and their surroundings",
       subtitle = "January to September 2025 compared with the same months of 2024") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2))
ggsave("take-home-02/figures/neighbour-changes.png", p_change_lag,
       width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 170, bg = "white")
```

![Township changes compared with the average change among Queen neighbours. The lines mark zero change; each dot is one township.](take-home-02/figures/neighbour-changes.png)

The changes have positive spatial clustering overall: **Moran’s I = `r round(as.numeric(change_moran$statistic), 3)`**, with permutation p = `r formatC(change_moran$p.value, format = 'f', digits = 3)`. Still, **`r sum(recent$change > 0 & recent$neighbour_change < 0, na.rm = TRUE)` of the `r sum(recent$change > 0 & has_neighbours)` rising townships with neighbours** sit beside an average decline.

Kyaukpyu added **207 events** while its neighbours averaged **53 fewer**. Nawnghkio also rose while its neighbours’ average fell. I would be cautious about assuming that the wider decline means less need for support in either township. The dot colours describe the direction of change; the earlier LISA and Gi* tests use totals for the whole study period.

### New hotspots appear around Kawkareik {#hotspots-in-two-periods}

The whole-period map combines several years of conflict, so a recent increase can be hard to see. Following the comparison of time windows in [Matthew Ho’s study](https://is415-gaa-matthew-ho.netlify.app/takehomeex/takehomeex2/the2#choosing-time-horizons), I repeat Gi* for January–September 2024 and January–September 2025. Both use the same Queen neighbours and 9,999 two-sided permutations, with p < 0.05. The extra permutations give finer p-values for this comparison.

```{r}
#| label: th02-period-hotspots
period_weights <- spdep::nb2listw(spdep::include.self(a$nb), style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
period_hotspots <- purrr::map_dfr(2024:2025, function(year) {
  counts <- recent[[paste0("events_", year)]]
  g <- spdep::localG_perm(counts, period_weights, nsim = 9999,
                        alternative = "two.sided", iseed = 62604,
                        zero.policy = TRUE, no_repeat_in_row = TRUE)
  p <- attr(g, "internals")[, "Pr(z != E(Gi)) Sim"]
  p[spdep::card(a$nb) == 0] <- NA_real_
  tibble(TS_PCODE = recent$TS_PCODE, year = year, events = counts,
         gi = as.numeric(g), p = p, q = p.adjust(p, "BH")) %>%
    mutate(hot = if_else(is.na(p), NA, gi > 0 & p < .05),
           hot_adjusted = if_else(is.na(q), NA, gi > 0 & q < .05),
           status = case_when(is.na(p) ~ "No Queen neighbour",
                              hot ~ "Hotspot", TRUE ~ "Not a hotspot"))
})
hotspot_changes <- period_hotspots %>%
  select(TS_PCODE, year, hot, hot_adjusted) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = c(hot, hot_adjusted)) %>%
  left_join(select(recent, TS_PCODE, TS, ST), by = "TS_PCODE") %>%
  mutate(change = case_when(
    is.na(hot_2024) ~ "No Queen neighbour",
    hot_2024 & hot_2025 ~ "Hotspot in both periods",
    hot_2025 ~ "Hotspot in 2025 only",
    hot_2024 ~ "Hotspot in 2024 only",
    TRUE ~ "Not a hotspot in either period"))
```

```{r}
#| label: th02-period-hotspot-maps
period_map <- a$towns %>%
  select(TS_PCODE) %>%
  left_join(period_hotspots, by = "TS_PCODE") %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  mutate(period = paste0(year, ": ", sum(hot, na.rm = TRUE), " hotspots"),
         status = factor(status, levels = c("Hotspot", "Not a hotspot", "No Queen neighbour")))
period_map <- ungroup(period_map)
kawkareik_point <- a$towns %>%
  filter(TS == "Kawkareik") %>%
  st_point_on_surface()
p_periods <- ggplot(period_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = status), colour = "white", linewidth = .08) +
  geom_sf(data = kawkareik_point, shape = 21, fill = "white", colour = "grey20", size = 2) +
  geom_sf_text(data = kawkareik_point, aes(label = TS), nudge_x = -45000,
               hjust = 1, size = 3.2, colour = "grey20") +
  facet_wrap(~period, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3, "Reds")[3], "grey90", "grey70"),
                    drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) + theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12)) +
  labs(title = "Hotspots around Kawkareik become clearer in 2025",
       subtitle = "January to September in each year · the circle marks Kawkareik")
ggsave("take-home-02/figures/hotspots-two-periods.png", p_periods,
       width = 10, height = 7.5, dpi = 170, bg = "white")
```

![Gi-star hotspots in January to September 2024 and the same months of 2025. Both maps use identical settings; Kawkareik is marked for orientation.](take-home-02/figures/hotspots-two-periods.png)

The hotspot count falls from **27 to 18**. Eleven townships are hotspots in both periods, 16 only in 2024, and seven only in 2025. **Five of those seven border Kawkareik**, where events rose from 122 to 356. In neighbouring Hlaingbwe, counts rose from just one to 41; all four of its neighbours also recorded increases.

For a needs assessment, I would include the surrounding townships as well as Kawkareik. The map describes a concentration across neighbours, which is why Kawkareik can sit beside hotspots without receiving the same label.

After adjusting for multiple tests, four hotspots remain in 2024 and three in 2025. Hlaingbwe is a 2025-only hotspot under both versions. These are changes in classification, not a direct statistical test of the change between years.

## How local patterns changed {#how-the-hotspots-changed}

The two-year comparison shows where hotspot labels changed. I now follow the monthly histories to understand when those changes took place. Kawkareik’s later increase and Monywa’s longer history of high counts are especially useful examples to keep in mind.

### Following hotspots through time


```{r}
#| label: th02-time-neighbours
#| eval: false
```

```{r}
#| label: th02-time-gi
#| eval: false
```

Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) uses each township and its Queen neighbours in the current and previous month. January 2021 uses January alone. Gi* compares these counts with the distribution across the whole space–time cube.


```{r}
#| label: th02-mann-kendall
#| eval: false
```

The **Mann–Kendall test** checks whether each township’s Gi* scores tend to rise or fall. It tracks the neighbourhood concentration; the event timelines show the township’s own counts.


```{r}
#| label: th02-classification-rules
#| eval: false
```

EHSA then combines that trend with the months classified as hot or cold. A new hotspot appears at the end for the first time; a consecutive hotspot has an uninterrupted final run; a sporadic hotspot appears on and off. Persistent, intensifying and diminishing hotspots require at least 90% of months to be hot. I use the same rules with the signs reversed for coldspots. [Classification definitions](https://doc.esri.com/en/arcgis-pro/latest/tool-reference/space-time-pattern-mining/learnmoreemerging.html)

### How hotspot patterns changed {#hotspots-came-and-went}


```{r}
#| label: th02-classify
#| eval: false
```

```{r}
#| label: th02-ehsa-plot
#| eval: false
```

![Mann–Kendall trends in space-time Gi-star scores and EHSA classifications, restricted to significant trend results.](take-home-02/figures/ehsa.png)

The full classification finds **26 oscillating hotspots and eight sporadic hotspots**. Of these, **16 and seven**, respectively, also have significant Mann–Kendall trends and appear on the map. No township meets the new, consecutive, persistent or intensifying hotspot rules in this run.

“Oscillating” has a specific meaning here: the township ends as a hotspot but has previously been a significant coldspot. It does not necessarily mean a regular cycle. “Sporadic” describes an on-and-off hotspot that ends hot and has no significant cold months.

The September 2025 endpoint affects the labels. Earlier hot months can still end in “No pattern detected” if the final-month rules are not met, as Monywa shows below.

Following the handout, the map shows **Mann–Kendall p < 0.05**.

### Coldspots also changed through time

The table includes all classifications, including those without a significant trend.

```{r}
#| label: th02-ehsa-counts
a$ehsa %>%
  group_by(classification) %>%
  summarise(`All townships` = n(), `Trend p < 0.05` = sum(trend_p < .05, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  rename(Pattern = classification) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

- **53 sporadic coldspots** include 20 in Yangon and 11 in Ayeyarwady. They were cold on and off, ended cold, and had no significant hot months.
- **12 persistent coldspots**, including 11 in Shan, were cold in at least 90% of months without a significant trend. The trend filter leaves them off the map above.
- **Matman, Mongping and Mongyawng are intensifying coldspots.** Their already low neighbourhood counts became more unusual relative to the whole study period as Gi* fell.
- **Kutkai is a consecutive coldspot:** its only two cold months came at the end, in August and September 2025.
- **Lashio, Tangyan and Laukkaing are oscillating coldspots.** They ended cold after earlier hot months. Only Laukkaing has a significant trend and appears in the map.

### Three townships, three different histories {#a-closer-look-at-contrasting-townships}

I take the highest-count township from each of the two hotspot classes with significant trends, plus Monywa for its largest overall total.


```{r}
#| label: th02-stories-plot
#| eval: false
```

![Monthly event counts and corresponding space-time Gi-star histories for contrasting township examples.](take-home-02/figures/township-stories.png)

**Kawkareik, Kayin (oscillating hotspot).** It had two coldspot months in 2021 before several later hotspot periods. By September 2025, it recorded **356 events for the year**, above the **168 in all of 2024**. Its rising Gi* trend passes the block-resampling check, showing a later concentration missed by the whole-period map.

**Nawnghkio, Shan (North) (sporadic hotspot).** Counts rose from five in 2021 to 310 in 2024 and 341 by September 2025. It has 18 hotspot months and no coldspot months. September had only four events, yet remained a hotspot because Gi* includes neighbours and the previous month.

**Monywa, Sagaing (no EHSA pattern at the endpoint).** It was a hotspot throughout 2022–2024 and in three of nine months in 2025. Its **1,039 events** are the largest historical total. September’s p-value of 0.066 misses the hotspot threshold; its Mann–Kendall trend is also not significant. I would still want to understand how households are recovering from the earlier violence.

### Do the trends hold up? {#checking-the-trend-results}

```{r}
#| label: th02-block-function
#| eval: false
```

```{r}
#| label: th02-block-run
#| eval: false
```

Nearby months are related, especially because Gi* includes the preceding month. I check the trend results with 999 resamples of six-month blocks after removing the estimated trend, then adjust for testing many townships.

The ordinary test identifies **`r sum(a$ehsa$trend_p < .05, na.rm = TRUE)` significant trends**. This falls to **`r sum(a$ehsa$block_p < .05, na.rm = TRUE)`** with the block check, and **`r sum(a$ehsa$block_q < .05, na.rm = TRUE)`** after also adjusting those block-test p-values across townships. The median correlation between successive Gi* scores is **`r round(median(a$ehsa$lag1, na.rm = TRUE), 2)`**, so treating the months as independent would overstate the evidence.

Kawkareik and Nawnghkio retain evidence of upward trends. Yesagyo does not: its p-value rises from about 0.006 to `r round(town_results$block_p[town_results$TS == 'Yesagyo'], 3)` in the block check, weakening the evidence for a sustained rise.

Adjusting the monthly hotspot tests and township trend tests also changes **`r sum(a$ehsa$classification != a$ehsa$classification_fdr)` EHSA classifications**. These labels depend on the significance settings, the neighbour definition and the chosen endpoint. The block check addresses short-term dependence approximately; seasonality and changes in reporting can still affect the results.

## Where civilians were targeted {#events-targeting-civilians}

The earlier comparisons include battles as well as attacks on civilians. For civilian assistance, I also want to know whether events targeting civilians followed the overall decline. I repeat the analysis for that subset and compare the places it brings into view.

### What the civilian records include


```{r}
#| label: th02-civilian-run
#| eval: false
```

The civilian-targeting flag selects **`r fmt(a$validation$civilian_records)` events**, or `r pct(a$validation$civilian_records/a$validation$retained)` of the retained records. This includes relevant bombings as well as “Violence against civilians”. Incidental harm is excluded; these counts describe events rather than deaths.

### Three hotspots appear only in the civilian map


```{r}
#| label: th02-civilian-plot
#| eval: false
```

![Comparison of Gi-star hotspots for all retained conflict records and for the subset targeting civilians.](take-home-02/figures/civilian-hotspots.png)

There are **37 civilian-targeting hotspots**, of which **34 overlap** the hotspots for conflict overall. The broad pattern is similar, but Hakha, Tonzang and Nawnghkio appear only in the civilian-targeting hotspot map. Myawaddy, Kyainseikgyi, Seikphyu and Mogoke appear only in the overall map.

Tonzang has only **two retained events targeting civilians**. Its hotspot label mainly reflects nearby townships, so an assessment needs to check where those incidents occurred.

### Little change in civilian targeting {#recent-civilian-targeting}

```{r}
#| label: th02-recent-civilian
recent_totals <- tibble(
  Measure = c("All retained conflict events", "Events targeting civilians"),
  `Jan–Sep 2024` = c(sum(recent$events_2024), sum(recent$civilian_2024)),
  `Jan–Sep 2025` = c(sum(recent$events_2025), sum(recent$civilian_2025))) %>%
  mutate(Change = scales::percent(`Jan–Sep 2025` / `Jan–Sep 2024` - 1, accuracy = .1))
knitr::kable(recent_totals, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

Events targeting civilians fell from **2,911 to 2,854**, a decline of just **2%**. Their share of retained events rose from **`r pct(sum(recent$civilian_2024)/sum(recent$events_2024))` to `r pct(sum(recent$civilian_2025)/sum(recent$events_2025))`**. Most of the national reduction came from events outside the civilian-targeting subset.

In **`r sum(recent$change < 0 & recent$civilian_change > 0)` townships**, total events fell while civilian-targeting events rose. Pakokku’s total dropped from 171 to 116, but civilian targeting rose from 15 to 35. Myaing had a similar pattern: total events fell from 180 to 103 while civilian targeting rose from 13 to 30. This is the finding that concerns me most when reading the national decline. I would keep both townships on the follow-up list for civilian assistance.

## Priorities for civilian assistance {#recommendations-and-limitations}

### Recommendations

The results draw attention to places where violence is increasing, as well as communities that have experienced years of conflict. I would use the maps to begin discussions with local aid groups about the following needs:

- **Find gaps in aid coverage in Sagaing, Mandalay and Magway.** They contain 31 of the 38 hotspots. Compare these townships with areas served by local aid groups, then prioritise communities still waiting for requested food, shelter or medical support.
- **Check for growing needs in Kawkareik, Kyaukpyu and Nawnghkio.** They had the three largest increases between the matched 2024 and 2025 periods. Include Hlaingbwe and the other townships bordering Kawkareik in these checks: the 2025 hotspot map points to a wider concentration there. Ask local groups whether displacement has increased demand for housing, food or care beyond what they can provide.
- **Include Kale and Maungdaw in local needs assessments.** They rank first and third for reported deaths. Ask local clinics and aid groups whether affected households have unmet care or support needs; Maungdaw would receive less attention on a list based only on incident counts.
- **Review Monywa’s needs before reducing existing aid.** It was a hotspot throughout 2022–2024. Check whether displaced households have housing, food and medical care alongside the recent fall in recorded events.
- **Follow up on civilian targeting in Pakokku and Myaing.** Their overall counts fell while events targeting civilians rose. Ask local groups whether affected households need medical care or shelter. For Hakha, Tonzang and Nawnghkio, also review neighbouring incidents behind the civilian hotspot labels.

The event records end in September 2025. Update them and confirm current needs with local aid groups before acting on this shortlist.

### Further study {#further-study}

Further study could follow Kyaukpyu and nearby townships month by month to see whether their rises and falls line up, while checking for changes in reporting. Comparing townships with similar totals could also reveal different patterns of violence and civilian targeting.

I would also like to understand whether communities facing rising civilian targeting can reach clinics and aid. Adding information on available services and travel times would help identify places where people face both violence and difficulty getting support.

### Limits of these maps

Counts depend on reporting coverage, approximate locations and township size. Fixed boundaries also leave out population movements and differences in exposure. The maps show where recorded events concentrate; explaining causes or judging present-day safety needs additional local evidence.
